day-1.t: Day 1 — Choose the subject and level that will actually sell

b.v: Today's goal

v: Pick a subject and level you can teach better than most
Check that parents are actually paying for it
Write a one-line offer a parent understands instantly

b.v: About 20 minutes. Running example: Ayesha in Karachi, teaches O-level mathematics, wants to replace a tuition job with her own students.

Most new online tutors say I teach all subjects, class 1 to 12. Parents do not search for that. They search for a specific need at a specific level, two weeks before an exam. The narrower your offer, the easier you are to find and the more you can charge.
1) Start from what you can teach well
There are three tests. If a subject fails the second or third, it will not become a business, however much you like it.

v: Can you teach it without preparation notes in front of you? That is competence
Can you explain the same idea three different ways? That is teaching
Can you name the five topics students fail most often? That is market knowledge
Ayesha passes all three in O-level maths and also in physics, but only maths has demand from her area

b.v: 2) Check demand before you build anything
Do not guess. Ask twenty parents and five students a direct question, and count the answers. This takes one week and prevents six months of empty slots.

Test demand in five days:|List 20 parents you can reach on WhatsApp, from your building, family and old students|Send one message: I am starting O-level maths online classes in small groups. What is the hardest part of maths for your child right now?|Count how many reply and how many name a real problem|Ask five of them what they pay now, and whether they would move for a better explanation|Decide: if fewer than six show real interest, change the subject or the level, not the price

v: Subjects with steady demand = maths, physics, chemistry, accounting, English writing, and exam-year classes
Levels with the most urgency = board exam years and the year before them
Avoid = subjects where the parent sees no measurable result, unless you can show one
Avoid = a level you have never studied. Parents spot it in the first lesson

b.v: 3) Write the one-line offer
Your offer is one sentence with four parts: what, who, how often, and the result. If your sentence has six parts, it is a menu, not an offer.

v: Weak = experienced teacher available for all classes, all subjects, reasonable fees
Strong = O-level maths, small group of four, three classes a week, aimed at a grade B or better in the May exam
Include the format, because parents now expect to know whether it is one-to-one or a group
Keep the same sentence everywhere: WhatsApp status, Facebook, and your profile description

b.v: The most common beginner mistake is pricing before choosing a specific student. A parent of a struggling class 8 student and a parent of a top O-level student need different things and will pay different amounts. Pick one type of student first, then set the price.
Practice
Write your one-line offer and send the demand-test message to twenty parents today. Keep the replies in a note, with the exact words they used about the problem. Their words become your marketing.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Pricing by hour and by month

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set an hourly rate and a monthly package
Price groups so that groups are worth the effort
Handle discounts without setting a bad precedent

b.v: About 25 minutes. Have a calculator and your real monthly costs.

Parents compare monthly totals, not hourly rates. You should decide in hours, because your time is the only thing you cannot buy more of, and then present in months, because that is what a household budget can plan for. Confusing the two is how tutors end up working 30 hours a week for a thin income.
1) Start from the number you need
Work backwards. Decide the monthly income you need, decide how many teaching hours you can actually do, and divide. Then check whether the market accepts that rate.

Do the arithmetic for Ayesha:|Target monthly income: Rs 60,000|Realistic teaching hours: 4 hours a day, 6 days a week = 24 hours a week, about 96 hours a month|Hours actually billable after cancellations: about 88|Required average rate: 60,000 ÷ 88 = about Rs 680 per hour|Market check: one-to-one O-level maths in her area is going at Rs 800 to 1,500 an hour, groups at Rs 350 to 600 per student|Decision: one-to-one at Rs 1,200 an hour, groups of four at Rs 500 per student per hour

v: Never count 96 hours as billable. Cancellations, no-shows and holidays eat 8 to 12 per cent
Your rate is per teaching hour, not per hour of your life. Preparation is inside the rate
A group of four at Rs 500 earns Rs 2,000 for the same hour. That is the whole point of groups
One-to-one at Rs 1,200 an hour with one student = Rs 1,200 for the hour
Group of 4 at Rs 500 each = Rs 2,000 for the same hour
Group of 6 at Rs 400 each = Rs 2,400 for the same hour
Group of 6 with two absent = Rs 1,600. Still better than one-to-one

b.v: 2) Present it as a monthly package
A monthly package makes the income predictable and stops the weekly fee conversation. State the number of classes so both sides know what they bought.

Build the package:|Count classes in the month: 3 a week for 4 weeks = 12 classes|One-to-one: 12 × Rs 1,200 = Rs 14,400. Price it at Rs 14,000 for a round number|Group: 12 × Rs 500 = Rs 6,000 per student|State what is included: classes, worksheets, one WhatsApp question window, a monthly progress note|State what is not included: extra classes outside the timetable, exam-day coaching, printed material

Do not charge per class only. Per-class pricing punishes you for a student's busy week and rewards nothing. A monthly package with a fixed class count protects your income and makes the parent commit.
3) Discounts that do not damage your price
Parents will ask. Have the answer ready, or you will invent one at the door and regret it.

v: Siblings = 15 per cent off the second child, not both
Advance payment = 5 per cent off for three months paid at once, because it improves your cash flow
Referral = one free class for the parent who refers, given after the new student pays
Never = a discount for asking twice. Say the price is the same for everyone, and hold it
Never = a discount in exchange for a good review. It cheapens both the review and the class

b.v: Practice

Calculate your required hourly rate from your income target and billable hours. Then write your monthly package for both one-to-one and group, with the class count and the inclusions. Save it as a note you can paste into WhatsApp in ten seconds.

day-3.t: Day 3 — A teaching setup that works on a phone

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a setup with what you already own
Fix the two things that ruin online lessons: sound and light
Have a backup plan for the day the internet dies

b.v: About 20 minutes. Test everything with a real student or a friend on a call.

Parents forgive a small screen. They do not forgive a lesson where they cannot hear you, cannot see the working, or where you disappeared for ten minutes. A good setup is not expensive, it is deliberate.
1) Phone, stand, light, sound
Four things, in order of importance. Most people spend money on the screen and ignore the sound, which is backwards.

v: Sound = wired earphones with a microphone, or a cheap clip mic. This matters more than the camera
Light = sit facing a window, never with the window behind you. A Rs 500 ring light is optional
Stand = a phone holder or a stack of books so the camera is at eye level, not looking up your nose
Screen = the phone you own. A tablet or laptop is better for writing, not essential for talking
Backdrop = a plain wall. Anything else becomes the topic of the lesson for a 12-year-old

b.v: Test your setup in 15 minutes:|Record a two-minute voice note of yourself explaining one concept|Play it back on earphones. Can you hear every word at low volume?|Join your own video call and check the light on your face|Show a page of your notebook to the camera. Is it readable?|Fix the worst of the four, and repeat next week
2) Write on screen without a fancy device
Maths, physics and accounting need visible working. You have three options, and one of them is a piece of paper.

v: Option 1 = a second phone or tablet held above a notebook, used as a document camera. Cheapest and often clearest
Option 2 = a shared whiteboard app inside the meeting, drawn on with a finger or a cheap stylus
Option 3 = write on paper and hold it up to the camera at the end of each step. Slow but works everywhere
Rule = the student must be able to copy the working. If they cannot, the method is wrong, not the student

b.v: Do not teach from a phone held in your hand for a whole lesson. The camera shakes, the student feels seasick, and you cannot write. A holder costs less than one class fee and fixes the biggest quality problem instantly.
3) The backup plan
Load-shedding and weak data are normal, not emergencies. What damages trust is silence. Have a written routine and tell parents about it in the first week.

Prepare three backups:|Data: keep a second SIM or a mobile hotspot ready, and know which network is stronger at your desk|Power: keep the phone charged above 60 per cent before every class, and have a power bank|Continuity: if the call drops for more than five minutes, send a WhatsApp voice note with the next task and reschedule the rest of the class within the same week
Practice

Record a two-minute explanation and check the sound. Then write your drop-out routine in three lines and keep it as a saved WhatsApp reply, so the next time the internet fails you send it in ten seconds instead of apologising for an hour.
Today's goal

v: Run a 45-minute lesson with a fixed shape
Keep a quiet student talking
End every class with proof of progress

b.v: About 20 minutes. Plan one real lesson while you read.

An online lesson fails differently from a classroom lesson. There is no room to fill, no board to lean on, and silence feels like a broken connection. A fixed structure carries you through, and it also tells the parent what they are paying for.
1) The 45-minute shape
Five parts, always in this order. The student should be talking for at least half the class, because talking is where understanding shows up.

Run the class like this:|Minutes 0 to 5: recall. Two questions from last lesson, answered out loud, no notes|Minutes 5 to 15: one new idea, explained three ways, with one example worked slowly|Minutes 15 to 30: the student does it. You watch and stay quiet for 30 seconds before helping|Minutes 30 to 40: fix the specific error you saw, then one harder question|Minutes 40 to 45: summary in the student's own words, then the homework, written in the chat

v: One new idea per class. Two ideas means neither is learned
Never explain for more than ten minutes without asking a question
Write the homework in the chat, not only spoken. Spoken homework disappears
Screenshot the last board and send it after class. It takes five seconds and looks professional

b.v: 2) Make the quiet student talk
Silence online is usually not rudeness. It is fear of being wrong in a room with no other faces to hide behind. Change the question, not the volume.

v: Ask a smaller question. Not solve it, but what is the first step?
Use a choice. Is the next step adding or multiplying?
Ask them to teach you. Explain to me how you got that, as if I were the student
Wait. Count to seven silently. Most students answer at five
Never fill the silence with the answer. It teaches them to wait

b.v: Do not race to finish the syllabus. Parents ask for coverage and then judge you by the exam result. A class that covers three topics badly is worth less than one that fixes one real misunderstanding, and the misunderstanding is what the exam will test.
3) End with proof
Every lesson should produce something visible that the parent can see without asking. This is what keeps students for a year instead of a month.

v: One photo of the finished working
One sentence from the student: today I learned that…
One mark: 4 out of 5 on today's practice questions
One next step, written and dated

b.v: Practice

Plan your next class in the five-part shape on one page. Write the two recall questions, the one new idea, the three ways you will explain it, and the homework. Then teach it and note which part ran over time.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Worksheets and homework that get done

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a worksheet in ten minutes
Set homework that students actually submit
Check work without marking for an hour

b.v: About 20 minutes. Bring one past paper or textbook chapter.

Homework is where learning happens and where tutoring businesses lose students. Too much and it is abandoned. Too little and the parent sees no value. Unchecked and the student learns that homework is decoration.
1) The ten-minute worksheet
Five questions, rising in difficulty, one of them from an old exam. That is a worksheet. Anything longer will not be done on a school night.

Build it:|Question 1: the exact example from class, with numbers changed|Question 2 and 3: same method, slightly different wording|Question 4: a question that mixes this topic with last week's|Question 5: one past-paper question, marked with the year|Type or write it clearly, photograph it, and send it as one image, not five

v: Keep a folder of past papers by topic. It is the most valuable asset in your business
Reuse worksheets with new numbers. Rewriting from scratch every week does not scale
One image per worksheet, named with the topic and date, so parents can find it later
Answer key written on a second page, sent after they submit

b.v: 2) Set homework so it gets done
Completion depends on three things: the deadline, the size, and whether someone looks. Get all three right and completion goes above 80 per cent.

v: Deadline = a specific day and time, not before next class
Size = under 25 minutes of real work. Say the time out loud
Look = you check it before the next class, every time, without exception
Say what happens if it is not done: the first ten minutes of the next class are used to finish it, not to teach new work

b.v: Do not give homework and then fail to check it. One unchecked week teaches the student that homework is optional, and you will spend the rest of the term chasing it. If you cannot check it, do not set it.
3) Check in five minutes, not fifty
You do not need to mark every line. You need to find the pattern of errors, because that is what the next class teaches.

Mark like this:|Ask for a photo of the work, not just the answers|Look for the same mistake twice. That is the pattern|Mark right or wrong only, no ticks and comments|Write one line: three of five correct, the sign error in question 4 repeats|Spend the first ten minutes of the next class on that one error|Send the parent one sentence: homework submitted, one recurring error being fixed
Practice

Build one five-question worksheet for your next topic, with the answer key on a second page. Set it with a specific deadline and a stated time limit, and check it before the next class. Note the completion rate. That number is your real teaching quality measure.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Talking to parents without losing your evenings

b.v: Today's goal

v: Send a weekly update that builds trust in four lines
Set communication boundaries in writing
Handle the difficult parent conversation

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write your update template and save it as a WhatsApp quick reply.

Parents are the customer, and the student is the user. If you only talk to the student, the parent decides whether to renew based on a vague feeling. A short weekly message, sent on the same day, turns that feeling into evidence.
1) The four-line weekly update
Send it every Thursday evening, for every student, in the same shape. It takes three minutes each and is the single best retention tool you have.

Use this template:|Covered this week: solving quadratic equations by factorising|Did well: set-up steps are now correct every time|Working on: sign errors when the constant is negative|Next week: completing the square, and a short test on Friday

v: Always include one thing going well, even in a bad week. It keeps the message readable
Be specific. Quadratic equations, not algebra
Send it even when there is nothing new. Consistency is the message
Never send it at midnight. Send between 6 and 9 pm

b.v: 2) Boundaries, said once and kindly

Without boundaries you will answer messages at 11 pm, teach a free class on Sunday, and start resenting the family that pays you. State the rules in the first week, in writing, before any problem exists.

v: Message window = 9 am to 8 pm, and I reply within a few hours
Class changes = 12 hours notice, otherwise the class counts as taken
Free extra classes = no. Extra classes are charged at the same rate
Fees = paid by the 5th of the month, in advance
Emergencies = call, do not message. Give the number and mean it

b.v: Do not give one family a special arrangement and expect the others not to hear about it. Tutoring runs on word of mouth, and a single exception becomes the standard within a month. Write the rules for everyone, and keep them.
3) The difficult conversation
Usually it is a parent worried about marks, or asking why the grade has not moved in three weeks. Have the facts ready and lead with the plan, not with defence.

Handle it in this order:|Acknowledge the worry in one sentence. Do not argue with the feeling|Show the evidence: attendance, homework completed, test scores over six weeks|Name the real cause, honestly. Sometimes it is effort, sometimes it is a gap from two years ago|Give a specific plan with a date: four weeks on fractions, then a test|Agree what the parent will do at home, usually 20 minutes of quiet and a homework check
Practice

Save the four-line update as a quick reply and send it to every current student this Thursday. Then send one message to each parent with your message window, change policy and fee date. Doing this now prevents three arguments later.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Trial classes that turn into students

b.v: Today's goal

v: Run a 25-minute trial that shows a real result
Ask for the decision clearly
Follow up without begging

b.v: About 25 minutes. Book one trial this week, even if it is free.
A trial class is not a sample of your personality. It is a small demonstration that the student can do something they could not do 25 minutes ago. Parents buy that feeling, not your qualifications.
1) The 25-minute trial shape
Short, focused, and built around one gap. Do not teach a normal lesson, and do not spend the time asking about goals.

Run it like this:|Minutes 0 to 3: one question to find the gap. What was the last maths topic you found easy?|Minutes 3 to 8: one diagnostic question at that level, watched silently|Minutes 8 to 18: teach exactly the missing step, then have them do one question alone|Minutes 18 to 22: a harder question that uses the new step. This is the proof moment|Minutes 22 to 25: tell the parent, in front of the student, what changed and what the next four weeks look like

v: Ask the parent to sit in for the last five minutes, if the child is comfortable
The proof moment must be a question the student could not do at minute five
Never spend the trial on a full chapter. You will run out of time and prove nothing
Take notes during the trial. Notes are what make the follow-up specific

b.v: 2) Ask for the decision, plainly
Most tutors end a trial with let me know and then wait. The parent is busy and slightly embarrassed to say no. Ask a clear question with a simple next step, and you will convert far more.

v: Say: the group has two seats left, one is Tuesday and Thursday at 5 pm and the other is Monday and Wednesday at 6 pm. Which suits you?
Give a choice between two times, not between yes and no
Say the fee and the start date in the same message
Hold the seat for 48 hours, then release it. Say that you will release it, and do

b.v: Do not offer a free month or a heavy discount to convert a trial. It tells the parent your normal price is not worth paying, and they will ask for the same discount again at renewal. Offer a paid trial month at the normal rate instead.
3) Follow up twice, then stop
One follow-up is polite. Two is professional. Three is pressure, and it costs you the referral even if it wins the student.

Follow up like this:|Same evening: a short message with one line on what the student achieved and the two time options|Day 3, if no reply: one message with a specific fact. The Tuesday seat is still open until Friday|Day 7, if no reply: we will keep your number and message you before the next intake. No more messages after that|Day 30: one message when a new group opens. That is all
Practice

Write your 25-minute trial plan with the diagnostic question and the proof question already chosen for your subject. Then write the follow-up message template, including the two time options and the fee, and save it as a quick reply.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Safety with children, and why it protects you too

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set rules that keep children safe online
Keep every conversation visible to a parent
Know what to do if something feels wrong

b.v: About 20 minutes. This lesson is not optional reading. Write your rules today.

You are an adult with private access to someone else's child, on a video call, sometimes for a year. That is a serious responsibility, and it is also a risk to your reputation if anything is ever misunderstood. Clear, written, visible rules protect the child first and you second. Never rely on being trusted. Rely on being transparent.
1) The five non-negotiable rules
Write these down, send them to every parent at enrolment, and follow them without exception, even when a parent says it is fine.

v: No private one-to-one chat with a minor. Every message goes in a group that includes a parent or guardian
No calls outside the scheduled class, and no calls after 8 pm, for any reason
No personal social media contact. Do not accept or send friend requests from students
No gifts, money, or favours to a student, and none accepted from them
No recording of a student without written consent from the parent, and no sharing of any recording with anyone else

b.v: Set up the channels properly:|Create one WhatsApp group per student, named Student name and parent|Add the parent and the student. Never message the student separately|Turn off disappearing messages, so the record stays|Post the class link only in that group, never in a public status|Keep messages about money in the same group, so the parent sees everything
2) Recording, consent, and privacy

Recording can be genuinely useful: a student who missed a class can watch it, and a parent can see what they are paying for. It can also be a serious privacy problem. Get consent in writing, and only record what you need.

v: Ask for written consent, in the group, before the first recorded class. Keep the message
Say exactly what is recorded: screen and voice, or camera too
Say who can watch it: the student and the parent only
Say when it is deleted: after 30 days, or after the exam
Never publish a class recording, even with faces blurred, without written consent

Follow the rules of your platform. Some countries and platforms have stricter rules on recording children, and local child protection law varies, so take professional advice if you plan to record regularly

b.v: The most dangerous habit is the friendly private chat. It starts with a homework question at 9 pm and becomes a relationship that no parent can see. Even with honest intentions, there is no record and no witness, and a single misunderstanding can end your business. Keep everything in the group. No exceptions, especially for your favourite student.
3) If something feels wrong
You may notice a change in a child: withdrawn, frightened, or talking about harm at home. You are not a counsellor and you must not investigate. Your job is to notice, record, and pass it on.

Do this, in order:|Write down what was said, in the child's exact words, with the date. Do not interpret|Do not question the child repeatedly, and do not promise secrecy|Tell the parent if the concern is about the online class or another adult online|If you believe a child is at risk at home, do not confront the family. Contact a child protection professional or the relevant authority and follow their guidance|Keep your own record of what you did and when
Practice

Write your five safety rules in plain language and send them to every current parent today, as a policy rather than a warning. Create one group per student with the parent included, and move any existing private student chat into it.
Today's goal

v: Set up JazzCash, Easypaisa and bank transfer properly
Send an invoice that gets paid on time
Keep records that show your real income

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this before your next fee cycle, not after.

Chasing fees is the most tiring part of tutoring, and it is entirely preventable. Most late payments are not refusals. They are a missing reminder, an unclear amount, or no way to pay that suits the parent. Fix the system and the awkwardness disappears.
1) Three ways to be paid, all of them easy
Give parents a choice, and make each option one step. The easier you are to pay, the faster you are paid.

v: JazzCash or Easypaisa = send the registered number and the exact name on the account, so the parent can verify it before sending
Bank transfer = send the account title, account number and bank name in one message, as text and not only as an image
Cash = only if you can give a written receipt immediately. Otherwise it becomes an argument in month three
Never = a personal account that is not in your name, unless the parent knows and agrees in writing

b.v: Set up collections in one afternoon:|Open a separate wallet or bank account for tuition income, so fees are never mixed with household money|Save the account details as a text snippet for fast sending|Write a standard invoice message with student name, month, class count, amount and due date|Send invoices on the 1st, with the 5th as the due date|Send one reminder on the 5th, and one on the 8th, then pause classes on the 10th
2) An invoice that gets paid
A good invoice removes every reason to delay. It states what was delivered, how much, and where to send it. One message, no attachments needed.

v: Student name and month = Ali Raza, November
What was delivered = 12 classes, worksheets, and the weekly progress updates
Amount = Rs 6,000
Due date = by 5 November
Payment details = JazzCash 03xx-xxxxxxx, account title Ayesha Khan
One line of thanks, no apology and no long explanation

b.v: Do not teach for two months without payment because you are shy. The longer the gap, the harder the conversation and the more likely you are never paid. Fees are in advance, the rule is written on day one, and the reminder is automatic. Being firm about money is not rude. It is professional.
3) Records that survive
You need to know what you actually earned, who has paid, and what is outstanding. Three columns in a notebook will do. Guessing will not.

v: Ali Raza, November, Rs 6,000, paid 3 November, balance 0
Hina Shah, November, Rs 6,000, paid 9 November, balance 0
Usman Tariq, November, Rs 14,000, not paid, balance Rs 14,000
One row per student per month. Never one row per year
One row per student per month. Never one row per year
Write the date the money actually arrived, not the date you sent the invoice
Keep the transaction ID or the transfer screenshot with the row
Total the month at the end and compare it with your bank or wallet statement
Keep these records for as long as your tax adviser tells you to. Ask them, because the requirement varies

b.v: Practice

Write your invoice message template and your written fee policy: in advance, due by the 5th, classes pause on the 10th, 12 hours notice for changes. Send both to every parent this week, before the next month starts.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Getting to a full timetable

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a weekly timetable that protects your energy
Fill empty slots with a referral engine
Raise your price when the timetable is full

b.v: About 25 minutes. Draw your timetable on paper, with real times.

A full timetable is not the same as a good business. Thirty scattered hours across seven days will exhaust you by month four and your teaching quality will fall, which is when students leave. Design the week on purpose.
1) Design the week before you fill it
Decide the shape first: which days, which hours, and how many total. Then sell only into those slots. Slots you never wanted are how resentment starts.

v: Six teaching days and one full day off. Protect the day off
4 hours a day, not 8. Online teaching is more tiring than it looks
Group similar levels back to back, so you prepare once for two classes
A 15-minute gap between classes covers the overrun and the messages
Leave Friday evening and one weekend morning free, and say so publicly
Monday to Thursday, 4 to 5 pm = Group 1, O-level maths
Monday to Thursday, 5.15 to 6.15 pm = Group 2, class 9 maths
Monday to Thursday, 6.30 to 7.30 pm = one-to-one
Friday = Group 1 and Group 2 only, evening free
Saturday = two one-to-one slots, then Group 3

b.v: 2) The referral engine that fills slots
You do not need advertising after the first ten students. You need a system that asks at the right moment, which is immediately after a visible win, not at the end of the year.

v: Ask after a result, not after a payment. That is when gratitude is highest
Use one sentence: your child moved from 45 to 62 in the class test. If you know a parent in the same position, I have one seat on Tuesday
Give the referrer something real: one free class, given after the new student pays
Ask the student too, quietly. Teenagers know exactly who is struggling
Keep two seats of capacity free at all times, so you can say yes the same week

b.v: Do not fill every hour and then accept one more student. A timetable with no gaps loses you one class every time a student needs to reschedule, and those lost classes eat 8 per cent of your income. Keep two slots a week unbooked on purpose.
3) When the timetable is full, raise the price
A full timetable with a waiting list means your price is too low. Raise it for new students first, and give existing students a date and a reason.

Raise it without losing people:|Wait until you have refused two students for lack of a seat|Raise the price for new students immediately. Existing students keep the old price for one term|Tell existing students 30 days before the increase, in writing, with one line of reason|Offer them the chance to pay three months in advance at the old rate|Expect one or two to leave. If nobody leaves, you waited too long

v: Track your average rate per teaching hour, not just total income
A tutor earning Rs 66,000 for 88 hours is earning Rs 750 an hour. That number is the one to grow
Moving one group from four students to six raises income without adding hours
Replace a low-paying slot with a group before you add a new day

b.v: Practice

Draw your real timetable for next week with actual times, including gaps and your day off. Count billable hours and multiply by your average rate to get your monthly gross. Then mark the two weakest slots and write the one action that would fill each.
